questions.prompt: Why does RunOnce cut both ways forensically?
options: It runs twice, doubling the evidence
It deletes its value after executing, giving the attacker a self-cleaning launcher but leaving the key's LastWriteTime as a trace
It cannot be used for persistence at all
questions.explanation: The self-deleting behavior removes the value before an investigator may see it, but the parent key's LastWriteTime still records when the modification occurred.

questions.prompt: Why does a Run key's LastWriteTime effectively date the persistence installation?
options: Registry values each carry their own timestamp
Registry keys carry a LastWriteTime but values do not, so the key's timestamp reflects when a value was last added or modified under it
LastWriteTime records the first boot of the system
It records when the key was last read
questions.explanation: Since only keys have timestamps, a Run key otherwise containing long-standing vendor entries has a LastWriteTime that points directly at the most recent change -- often the malicious addition.

questions.prompt: Why must the Wow6432Node variants be checked separately?
options: They are aliases that always mirror the native keys
They are genuinely separate keys used by 32-bit software on 64-bit Windows, so checking only the native path misses entries written there
They only exist on Windows Server
They are deprecated and never used
questions.explanation: 32-bit applications on 64-bit Windows are redirected to Wow6432Node, making it a distinct location that a native-path-only check will not cover.

questions.prompt: Which Autoruns options most effectively reduce a long autostart list to a reviewable one?
options: Sorting alphabetically and filtering by date
Hide Microsoft entries, combined with Verify code signatures
Exporting to CSV and opening in Excel
questions.explanation: Hiding signed Microsoft entries and verifying signatures on what remains collapses roughly a hundred autostart locations into a short list actually worth reading.
